questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish master data from transactional data?
options: Master data is the core, slow-changing entities (like customers or products) that transactional data references rather than duplicating
Master data only ever exists in Salesforce, never in any other system
Transactional data is always more important to the business than master data
There is no meaningful difference -- the two terms describe the same thing
questions.explain: Master data (customers, accounts, products, vendors) is the core entity that transactional data (an order, a case, an invoice line) references, rather than re-describing, each time a transaction occurs.

questions.q: What does this lesson define a 'golden record' as?
options: The very first record ever created for an entity in any system
The single, trusted, agreed-upon version of a master data entity's core attributes, reconciled across the systems that each hold their own copy
A record that has been manually flagged as important by an administrator
A record that exists only in the ERP and nowhere else
questions.explain: A golden record is the reconciled, trusted version of an entity's core attributes that the enterprise agrees is correct, even though individual systems may still keep their own local operational copies.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is producing a golden record an automatic process?
options: No -- it requires matching records across systems with different identifiers and deciding which system's value wins when systems disagree
Yes -- golden records are generated automatically the moment two systems are integrated
Yes -- any system with the most records automatically becomes the golden-record source
Golden records only apply to transactional data, never to master data
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that getting to a golden record requires matching across differing identifiers and resolving conflicts when systems disagree -- it is not automatic just because systems are connected.

questions.q: In the typical enterprise example this lesson gives, which system is described as usually the system of record for the core legal/billing identity of a customer, as opposed to the sales-relationship facts about that same customer?
options: Salesforce, for both the legal/billing identity and the sales-relationship facts
The ERP or a dedicated MDM platform for legal/billing identity, with Salesforce as the system of record for sales-relationship facts like territory assignment
A marketing automation platform for the legal/billing identity
No system is ever responsible for legal/billing identity
questions.explain: The lesson describes a typical split where the ERP or MDM platform owns the legal/billing identity while Salesforce owns sales-relationship facts such as primary sales contact, account tier, and territory assignment for that same customer.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens when no system is explicitly designated as the master data owner for an entity?
options: Nothing changes -- master data self-organizes correctly without explicit ownership
Each system tends to quietly treat itself as authoritative, recreating the 'dueling systems of record' problem at the scale of the enterprise's most heavily referenced entities
Salesforce automatically becomes the default owner in every case
The data simply stops being referenced by any transactional record
questions.explain: Without an explicit ownership decision, the common failure is each system independently assuming it's authoritative -- the same dueling-systems-of-record failure from Lesson 3, but now affecting the enterprise's most widely referenced entities.
